verdict.reasoning: Patient reports noticing the swelling "about a week ago" and confirms it is the left elbow: "I just noticed this like about a week ago... have like a weird swelling on... my elbow" and later "it's the, the left elbow."
Patient describes: "It's not painful at all" and "it's slightly warm" and "I, I, cannot feel like this, little bit fluid in inside" about the left elbow.

Patient states: "I can actually like move it normally" and denies trauma: Doctor asks "have you banged that elbow? Do you have any kind of injury?" Patient: "No, not really... I haven't noticed anything."
Doctor asks "has this happened before?" Patient replies: "No, no I haven't noticed that before. Um, I don't have any like history of, of seeing this."
Patient says: "I think I have something like uh, osteoarthritis" and later confirms prior diagnosis: Doctor: "Has anyone ever told you that?" Patient: "Yes. Yes, a few years ago."
Patient states: "I'm, I'm allergic to, to peanuts."
Doctor asks: "are, are you allergic to any medication?" Patient: "Uh, no. Not that I know of."
Doctor asks: "do you um, are you on any medication on a regular basis?" Patient: "Uh, no."
Doctor asks about family rheumatology diseases; patient replies regarding family: "in my family, I'm not sure" then "No." indicating no known family history.
Regarding job: "No, I just, you know sit at a desk." Regarding exercise: "I run regularly, like two, three times a week."
Smoking and alcohol use are not mentioned anywhere in the transcript; stating they are not mentioned is consistent with the record.

Swelling over olecranon of left elbow is implied by visual exam and earlier description of swelling at elbow tip; warmth is confirmed: "It's a bit warm, yes." Tenderness over swelling: patient says pressing "where the, the swelling is, it's a bit, yeah it feels weird."

Doctor notes: "I noticed the skin was a bit dry, on the tip of the elbow." No marked erythema is consistent with absence of any mention of redness on exam and later statement that it does not look like septic arthritis. Full active range of motion supported by patient: "I can actually like move it normally."

Doctor states: "this seems like uh, what we call the Bursitis" of the elbow, and later: "It doesn't look like... septic arthritis" and "this is not the case right now... it looks quite straightforward," indicating non-septic bursitis.

Doctor plans blood tests "to check for other types of uh, causes of joint swelling" including "inflammatory markers, infection, rheumatological antibodies" and "also check for things like Gout as well," which corresponds to ruling out gout and systemic inflammatory arthropathy.

Doctor advises: "I would take Ibuprofen regularly... that's four hundred milligrams, two times a day. And you should take, take that after food, not on an empty stomach. If you get any heartburn, stop taking it."

Transcript mentions blood tests for "inflammatory markers, infection, rheumatological antibodies" and "Gout" but does not specify FBC, ESR/CRP, urate or a full infection screen by name; these specific panels are additional detail not stated.

Doctor explains: "results will come back to us after about five or six days" and notes if the patient gets tests done straight away, "we're looking maybe six days." This matches results expected in approximately 6 days; "ASAP" is consistent with "if you get the form get the blood tests done straight away."

Doctor: "we can arrange a follow-up appointment for you..." and later: "the follow-up appointment doesn't have to be face-to-face... we can do that over the phone, uh, over video. We can do that as well."

Doctor advises: "if your, the elbow was to become very red, very painful, uh, and the redness was to spread or become uh, you know more intense. Then you need to get on the phone or get... a video appointment... as soon as possible" and notes this could indicate septic arthritis requiring emergency assessment.
